Aggregated opinion polling for the next Australian federal election, set against the last five. Labor leads the Coalition 52–48 two-party preferred (±2.7) – updated 30 August 2026 from 155 published polls across 12 polling houses. Next election due by 20 May 2028.

Labor leads by 4 points. The aggregate is a sample- and recency-weighted, house-effect-adjusted mean over a 21-day window (7-day half-life), carrying a 95% interval of ±2.7 points from 5 polls. About this tracker

auspol tracker pools every published national voting-intention poll since the May 2025 federal election. The two-party and primary-vote aggregates are weighted means: recent and larger polls count for more, and each pollster’s figure is adjusted for its own lean against the consensus of all houses. The lean is measured separately for every measure – a firm that leans one way on the classic two-party is not assumed to lean the same way on a primary share or an ALP-v-One Nation head-to-head – and a matchup too few houses ask is left as a plain monthly average rather than adjusted on guesswork. The leaders’ ratings and national direction run through the same monthly weighting and adjustment; preferred prime minister and the undecided share stay as plain averages, the differences there being a matter of question wording rather than lean. Houses that publish no two-party figure feed the primary-vote and leadership series only.

The headline carries a 95% interval – the greater of the spread among polls in the window and their sampling error – currently about ±2.7 points on 5 polls across 21 days (effective sample 4.2 after weighting). It cannot cover error the whole industry shares: an aggregate has no way to see a lean every poll in it carries. Movement smaller than the interval is marked as such.

That caveat is not idle. Across the 5 elections from 2013 to 2025 the final polls missed the two-party result by 1.2 points on average – at 2019 by 2.9, every house on the same side of it. Past cycles carries the full record, house by house.

Reading the charts

Each dot is one published poll; the lines are monthly aggregates, shaded with the 95% interval around them. Where the two bands meet, that month’s lead is inside its own margin of error. Leadership questions are asked irregularly, so those lines are monthly aggregates too – adjusted per house for approval and favourability, joined straight from published readings for preferred prime minister. A “—” in any table means the pollster didn’t ask that question.

Why there is no seat projection here. Turning a national two-party figure into a seat count assumes a uniform swing, and with One Nation near 26% of the primary vote the assumption fails in exactly the seats that would decide the election: a large minor party wins seats where its vote is concentrated and none where it is not – and no national number knows the difference. Seat figures appear on this page only where a pollster modelled them seat by seat and published the result, which is what the MRP tag in the archive marks.
